stories.title: Germany gives sweeping powers to police, intelligence services
stories.summary: Drone sightings and cyberattacks have heightened security concerns. How are the police preparing to meet these challenges? And how do intelligence services plan to counter threats from both domestic and foreign sources?
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PQR9 Prefer DW on Google Cybercrime can also affect supermarkets, like Irish chain SuperValu whose cooling systems were hacked in early November Image: REUTERS Advertisement Germany's intelligence agencies have been given wide-ranging new powers. The lawmakers in the Bundestag agreed to a reform package on Friday. Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Germany's foreign intelligence service, will be allowed to respond to cyberattacks by foreign powers with counterattacks of its own. The range of possible measures is broad, from deleting and manipulating data to disabling entire systems and, if necessary, even destroying physical weapons such as drones that could be deployed against Germany. Under certain conditions, the agencies will also be permitted to enter homes and business premises covertly, for example, to prepare surveillance operations. They will, however, not be allowed to use force against people. An independent oversight board is to be established to monitor the agencies. Opposition lawmakers specializing in domestic policy warned against granting powers that are too broad.

"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas. The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower. But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea. The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:20 local time (21:20 GMT) on Saturday, in the first-ever successful catch attempt. stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PITB Prefer DW on Google Image: DW Advertisement High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a new study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues. Across 826 people in the United States and China , women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores did not receive such treatment, and in one group, they were treated better. The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men. Since it was published this year, Nitya Chawla, an associate professor at UCL School of Management in London and the researcher behind the study, says women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility. How was the study done, and what are its limits? The researchers ran two studies.
